ASNT Level III consulting in the USA: what you are buying

ASNT Level III consulting gives a US company the technical authority SNT-TC-1A expects a Level III to provide, without hiring one full time. A consultant writes or fixes the written practice, prepares and approves NDT procedures and technique sheets, runs or oversees qualification examinations, reviews certification records and prepares you for client audits. The employer still certifies its own people. The consultant supplies the Level III work behind that certification.

Atlantis NDT runs this work from Houston. Most of it is remote document work, with site visits when an audit, a practical examination or a new technique needs someone in the room. If you already know you need help, talk to a Level III and send the current written practice with your first email.

What NDT consulting covers, and what it does not

"NDT consulting" is used loosely. Some firms mean inspection staffing. Some mean engineering assessments. Under SNT-TC-1A, it means the Level III functions an employer needs and does not have in-house. Those functions are narrow and specific, which makes them easy to scope.

ServiceWhat you receiveTypical trigger
Written practice authoring or rewriteA revision-controlled written practice covering every method and level you use, with training, experience, examination, vision and recertification rules stated as "shall"New company, new method, client rejection, or an old document nobody can defend
Procedures and technique sheetsMethod procedures tied to the code edition your contracts name, plus technique sheets for specific geometries, materials and thicknessesA new client spec, a new code edition, or a technique being improvised in the field
ExaminationsGeneral, specific and practical examinations, answer keys, grading records and specimens matched to your workLevel I or II candidates ready to certify, or recertification falling due
Record reviewA check of every certification file against your own written practice: hours, exam grades, vision, signatures, expiryPre-audit, after an acquisition, or after losing the person who kept the files
Internal and pre-client auditsA findings list against the written practice, procedures and the client's checklist, with corrective actionsClient prequalification, a supplier audit, or an ISO 9001 surveillance visit
Outsourced Level IIIOngoing Level III responsibility for the methods in scope, named in your written practice, on a defined review cycleNo in-house Level III, or one Level III who does not cover every method you use

What US NDT consulting from Atlantis does not include is just as important. We do not perform risk-based inspection studies to API 580/581. We do not perform fitness-for-service assessments to API 579. We are not the API Authorized Inspector on your vessels, piping or tanks. On API 510, 570 and 653 work, the owner's Authorized Inspector stays the inspector of record. A Level III consultant makes sure the NDE behind that inspector's decisions is done to a qualified procedure by qualified people. That is a different job, and mixing the two up is one of the most common reasons a consulting scope goes wrong.

The US rules that drive the work

US NDT personnel qualification is employer-based. There is no state NDT licence and no federal certificate for a UT or MT technician. Instead, codes and regulations require "qualified" personnel and point back to an employer program. The written practice is where those requirements land.

  • SNT-TC-1A and CP-189. SNT-TC-1A is ASNT's recommended practice. The 2024 edition has replaced the 2020 edition. An employer adopts it through a written practice in which "should" becomes "shall". ANSI/ASNT CP-189 is the national standard alternative, used where a contract or a nuclear code calls for it.
  • ASME Section V. Construction and in-service codes that reference Section V expect examinations to follow written procedures, performed by personnel qualified under the employer's written practice. A procedure that does not name the code edition it was written to is a frequent audit finding.
  • OSHA process safety management. At covered refineries and chemical plants, 29 CFR 1910.119(j) requires inspection and testing of process equipment to follow recognised and generally accepted good engineering practice, and requires each inspection to be documented. Your NDT program is part of the evidence the owner relies on.
  • PHMSA pipeline rules. For gas pipelines, 49 CFR 192.243 requires nondestructive testing of welds to be performed in accordance with written procedures, by persons trained and qualified in those procedures and with the equipment used. That one sentence is why pipeline clients ask for your procedure and your technician's qualification record together.
  • API in-service codes. API 510 (11th edition, 2022), API 570 (5th edition, February 2024) and API 653 (with Addendum 4, July 2025) set what the Authorized Inspector needs from the examiner. The examiner's employer keeps the certification records. The consultant's job is to make those records hold up.
  • Jurisdictional overlays. Many states adopt the National Board Inspection Code for boiler and pressure vessel repairs. That does not change how NDT technicians are certified, but it changes which documents an inspector expects to see on a repair package.
  • Aerospace. Aerospace primes and Nadcap audits work to NAS 410 and customer specifications. NAS 410 has its own Level 3 rules. Confirm with your prime which Level 3 qualification it accepts before you engage any consultant for an aerospace program.

How a US consulting engagement runs, step by step

  1. Scoping call. We ask which methods you use, which levels you certify, which codes your contracts name and what triggered the call. A client rejection is scoped differently from a new company setting up its first program.
  2. Document intake. You send the written practice, the procedure list, a sample of certification files and any client audit findings. Anonymised copies are fine at this stage.
  3. Gap review. We mark up the written practice against SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 and against your client specs. Each gap is listed with the clause it fails and the fix.
  4. Quote. You get a fixed scope and a quote within 24 hours of the gap review, either as a project or as a retainer.
  5. Drafting. We rewrite the written practice and the procedures that need it. Technique sheets follow for the geometries that are causing trouble.
  6. Working session. We walk your operations manager and senior Level IIs through the changes. This is where the document becomes yours instead of ours.
  7. Approval and issue. The Level III approves the procedures and the written practice is issued under revision control. Old revisions are withdrawn, not left on the shared drive.
  8. Examinations. General, specific and practical examinations are prepared and administered or overseen. Grades, specimens used and the examiner's name go into each file.
  9. Audit support. Before a client or registrar audit, we run a mock audit against their checklist. During the audit, the Level III answers technical questions.
  10. Ongoing cover. On a retainer, procedure revisions, new hires, method extensions and code edition changes are handled on an agreed review cycle.

Steps 1 to 4 are the same for every client. Steps 5 to 10 are picked from as needed. A company that only needs a procedure pack for one new client may stop at step 7.

Consulting and training meet at the written practice. It sets the training hours, training supplies them, the Level III examines and the employer certifies. See how employer-based NDT training in the USA uses the same document, how written practice development works clause by clause, and what an outsourced Level III signs on the ASNT Level III consulting services page.

Who uses an NDT Level III consultant in the US

The question is not company size. It is whether you have Level III coverage for every method you put your name to. These are the buyers we see most often.

  • Small NDT service companies. They certify their own Level I and II people but cannot keep a full-time Level III busy. An outsourced Level III is named in the written practice and covers the methods they sell.
  • Contractors who lost their Level III. Resignation, retirement or a dispute can leave a company with certificates signed by someone who no longer works there. The program has to be picked up before the next recertification or client audit.
  • Fabrication shops adding a method. A shop that has run VT and MT for years and now needs UT for ASME Section VIII or AWS D1.1 work needs a UT procedure, a UT section in the written practice and qualified examiners before the first job.
  • Mid-size contractors moving into PAUT and TOFD. Advanced UT brings technique qualification and scan plans that a conventional UT Level III may not cover. The consultant fills the method gap without replacing the in-house Level III.
  • Owner-operators with in-house inspection crews. Refineries, chemical plants and pipeline operators that run their own NDT crews need the same written practice discipline as a contractor, and often an independent review before a PSM audit.
  • Companies facing client prequalification. Major operators and EPCs review your written practice and a sample of technician files before they approve you. Fixing the program first is cheaper than failing the prequalification.

How to compare NDT Level III consultants

Most buyers compare consultants on rate. Rate matters, but it is rarely what goes wrong. These are the questions that separate a consultant who will hold up at audit from one who will not.

Question to askA good answerA warning sign
Which methods does your ASNT NDT Level III certificate cover?A list that matches every method in your scope, which you can check with ASNT"We cover all methods" with no detail
Will you be named in our written practice?Yes, with the scope, authority and review cycle written downAdvice only, no signature, or a signature with no defined duties
Which code editions do you write procedures to?The edition your contract names, stated on the procedureA template procedure with no edition
How are examinations run when you are remote?Controlled papers, a named proctor, practical exams on your specimens, records kept by youOpen-book online quizzes graded by nobody
Who keeps the records?You do. The consultant reviews and signs, the employer owns the filesThe consultant holds your records and you cannot see them
What happens if a client challenges a result?A Level III review of the data and procedure, with a written answer"Send it back to the technician"
What do you not do?A clear list, for example no FFS, no RBI, not the Authorized InspectorNothing is outside scope

Ask for a sample deliverable with client names removed. A marked-up written practice tells you more about a consultant than a capability statement does.

Common mistakes in US NDT programs

  • Copying another company's written practice. It names methods you do not use and leaves out the ones you do. Auditors notice the mismatch quickly.
  • Using SNT-TC-1A's "should" as if it were optional. Once adopted into your written practice, the requirements are "shall". You are audited against your own document.
  • Procedures with no code edition. A UT procedure written "to ASME" without an edition cannot be checked against the contract.
  • A Level III name with no evidence of work. If the Level III approved a procedure, there should be a dated approval. If they graded an exam, their name should be on the grade sheet.
  • Treating a training certificate as certification. A course certificate is evidence of training hours. Certification is issued by the employer after experience and examinations.
  • Lapsed vision records. An expired vision examination undermines an otherwise valid certificate. It is the cheapest finding to avoid.
  • An outside Level III not described in the written practice. If you use one, the written practice should say so and define the arrangement.
  • Informal technique approval. A scan plan made up on the job for an awkward nozzle is a nonconformance waiting to be found.

Many of these surface in the record review. Certificate expiry dates, vision dates and exam grades are easier to keep straight when they live in a system that warns you before they lapse. The NDT personnel certification tracking page shows how Atlantis ERP handles that.

Behind the consulting work sit 1,500+ inspection activities and 1,000+ technicians trained. Our founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, is an ASNT NDT Level III. To scope a written practice, a procedure pack or outsourced Level III cover, talk to a Level III.

Canada notes for US companies working across the border

Canada does not use the US employer-based model for most code work. Personnel are commonly certified as individuals through a national scheme. The CGSB closed its NDT certification activity on 1 April 2026. Natural Resources Canada's NDT Certification Body continues and issues certification to CAN/CGSB-48.9712. A US contractor sending SNT-TC-1A certified technicians into Alberta or Ontario should confirm early whether the owner or the jurisdiction requires that national certification. Procedures and written practices can still be prepared to cover both. The Canada consulting page covers the details.

Frequently asked questions

What does ASNT Level III consulting include?

It covers the Level III functions an employer needs under SNT-TC-1A or CP-189: writing or revising the written practice, preparing and approving procedures and technique sheets, preparing and administering or overseeing examinations, reviewing certification records and supporting audits. It can be a one-off project or an ongoing outsourced Level III arrangement.

Can an outside NDT Level III consultant act as our Level III?

Yes, when the arrangement is written into your written practice. The employer remains the certifying authority and keeps the records. The outside Level III provides the technical functions on a defined scope and review cycle. That split has to be clear on paper, or it will not survive an audit.

What is the difference between NDT consulting and NDT Level 3 consulting services?

In practice, buyers use the terms for the same thing. Strictly, NDT Level 3 consulting services are the Level III functions: written practice, procedures, examinations and records. Broader NDT consulting may also include inspection planning or report review. Atlantis does not offer RBI or fitness-for-service assessments.

Do we need the consultant on site?

Not for most work. Written practices, procedures, technique sheets and record reviews are done remotely. Practical examinations, mock audits and new technique trials are usually better on site. We scope the site days when we scope the work.

How is NDT consulting priced in the US?

Quote on request. Scope drives it: how many methods, how many procedures, whether examinations are included and whether you want a project or a retainer. We send a quote within 24 hours of the scoping call or gap review.

Does a Level III consultant replace our API Authorized Inspector?

No. On API 510, 570 and 653 work, the owner's Authorized Inspector remains the inspector of record. The Level III makes sure the NDE behind the inspector's decisions is done to approved procedures by qualified personnel.

Can you get us ready for a client audit or prequalification?

Yes. We review the written practice, procedures and a sample of technician files against the client's checklist, list the gaps with fixes and run a mock audit. A Level III can attend the audit itself to answer technical questions.

Which US states do you cover?

All of them. Our US office is in Houston. Document work is remote, and site visits are arranged to your location. The state hubs above cover the industries and client requirements in each state.
